label: PYQ-style
stem: Is the third level a real place or a medium of escape from the harsh realities of modern life? Discuss with reference to the story. (120–150 words)
hint: Sam's view and its support → evidence for reality (details, clerk, cover, Sam's disappearance) → Finney's ambiguity → theme.
model_answer:
Finney builds the story so that both readings stand. Sam the psychiatrist calls the third level a waking-dream wish fulfilment: Charley is unhappy in a world of insecurity, fear, war and worry, and Galesburg of 1894 — long peaceful evenings on wide lawns — is the refuge his mind has invented. The reading fits: Charley stumbles on the level while lost in Grand Central's maze, and he can never find the corridor again. Even his stamp collecting is, in Sam's words, a temporary refuge from reality.

Yet the story resists this. The period details are exact, the clerk's suspicion of modern money is not what one dreams, and the first-day cover is a physical object with Sam's handwriting and an 1894 postmark. Sam really has disappeared, and the coin dealer confirms he bought eight hundred dollars of old currency.

Whether real or imagined, the third level stands for the universal wish to escape the pressures of the present into a simpler, safer past — which is the story's true subject.

scheme.step: Sam's view and the evidence supporting escape/fantasy
Evidence for reality: details, clerk, first-day cover, Sam's disappearance and purchase
Conclusion on ambiguity and the theme; expression and length

label: PYQ-style
stem: Sam, who explained away Charley's experience, ends up on the third level himself. Trace Sam's role in the story and explain the irony of the ending. (120–150 words)
hint: Diagnosis → Louisa's objection → disappearance → first-day cover letter → 800 dollars, feed business → irony.
model_answer:
Sam enters the story as the voice of reason. A psychiatrist and Charley's friend, he explains the third level as a waking-dream wish fulfilment: Charley is unhappy, the modern world is full of insecurity, fear, war and worry, and he wants to escape. When Louisa bristles, Sam softens it — everyone wants to escape, even a stamp collector seeks a temporary refuge from reality.

Then Sam vanishes. In his grandfather's stamp collection Charley finds a first-day cover postmarked Galesburg, July 18, 1894, containing a letter in Sam's handwriting: he has found the third level, Galesburg is as lovely as Charley said, and Charley and Louisa should keep looking. The coin dealer confirms Sam bought eight hundred dollars of old-style currency — enough, Charley notes, for a hay, feed and grain business.

The irony is complete: the man who diagnosed the escape wish has escaped, and he could never resume his old profession, for a psychiatrist has no clients in a town without worry.

The irony explained (sceptic escapes; psychiatrist useless in 1894)
